questions.title: Measuring instruments, scales, bricks and baking

subQuestions.questionText: Choose an item from COLUMN B that matches the description in COLUMN A. The most appropriate scale to draw a map of South Africa. Options: A (scale bar 0–200 km), B (tape measure), C (circular saw), D (1 : 50 000), E (vernier caliper), F (ruler 0–10 cm), G (1 cm = 1 m).
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D — 1 : 50 000 (2 marks)
Accept 1 : 50 000.

subQuestions.questionText: The instrument most suited to measure the circumference of a dinner plate. Choose from COLUMN B (A–G).
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: E — Vernier caliper (2 marks).
[Note: memo states E; per attached notes also accept B (tape measure).]

subQuestions.questionText: The most appropriate scale to draw a plan of a house. Choose from COLUMN B (A–G).
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: G — 1 cm = 1 m (2 marks).
Accept 1 cm = 1 m.

subQuestions.questionText: The instrument most suited to measure the width of a soccer field. Choose from COLUMN B (A–G).
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: C (2 marks). [Per attached notes: also accept B — tape measure.]

subQuestions.questionText: The instrument most suited to measure the length of a pencil. Choose from COLUMN B (A–G).
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: F — Ruler (0 – 10 cm) (2 marks). [Per attached notes: accept E or B.]

subQuestions.questionText: A standard brick has Height = 70 mm, Width = 112 mm, Length = 240 mm. State which formula (A, B or C) below can be used to calculate the total surface area (TSA) of the given brick. A: TSA = Area of front side + Area of right-hand side + Area of top. B: TSA = $(2 \times 240 \times 70 + 2 \times 240 \times 112 + 2 \times 112 \times 70)$ mm². C: TSA = $(240 \times 70 + 240 \times 112 + 112 \times 70)$ mm².
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
Formula B correctly accounts for all six faces of the rectangular brick (each pair of opposite faces multiplied by 2).

options.A: TSA = Area of front side + Area of right-hand side + Area of top

subQuestions.questionText: State the unit of measurement for the volume of this brick.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: $\text{mm}^3$ OR cubic millimetres (2A correct unit).
Accept cubic centimetres ($\text{cm}^3$) for full marks.

subQuestions.questionText: Convert the length of this brick (240 mm) to metres.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Length} = \frac{240}{1000}$ (1C correct conversion factor — divide by 1 000)
Mark 2: $= 0{,}24$ m (1A simplification)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the maximum number of rows of bricks that can be stacked height-wise to a height of 2 100 mm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Numerator $= 2\,100$ mm (1A height)
Mark 2: Denominator $= 70$ mm (1A correct denominator)
Mark 3: Number of rows $= \frac{2\,100\,\text{mm}}{70\,\text{mm}} = 30$ (1CA number of rows)
[CA only applies if 1 value is correct, i.e. either 2 100 or 70 must have been used in a fraction; max 2 marks if simplified correctly with one correct value.]

subQuestions.questionText: Maria uses a recipe (makes 1 dozen scones) that includes 500 g flour. Convert the mass of the flour to kilograms.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\frac{500}{1\,000}$ (1C divide by 1 000)
Mark 2: $= \frac{1}{2}$ kg or $0{,}5$ kg (1A simplification)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the number of large eggs needed to make 30 scones. (Recipe: 2 large eggs makes 1 dozen = 12 scones.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1:
Mark 1: 12 scones = 2 eggs, so 6 scones = 1 egg (1A dozen = 12)
Mark 2: 30 scones = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 eggs (1A simplification)

OR Method 2:
Mark 1: 12 scones = 2 eggs (1A dozen = 12)
Mark 2: 30 scones $= \frac{30}{12} \times 2 = 5$ eggs (1A simplification)

OR Method 3:
Mark 1: 30 scones $= \frac{30}{12} = 2{,}5$ dozen (1A dozen = 12)
Mark 2: 1 dozen needs 2 eggs, so $2{,}5 \times 2 = 5$ eggs (1A simplification)

subQuestions.questionText: Each scone has an average diameter of 7 cm. Write down the average radius of EACH scone.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Radius $= 7$ cm $\div 2$ (1MA dividing by 2)
Mark 2: $= 3{,}5$ cm OR $35$ mm (1A radius)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate how many full dozen scones can be made with 500 g of butter. (Recipe uses 75 g butter for 1 dozen.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\frac{500}{75}$ (1MA dividing by 75)
Mark 2: $= 6{,}67$ (1S simplification)
Mark 3: $= 6$ full dozen (1R rounding down)

subQuestions.questionText: The scones were placed in the oven to bake at 14:10. Write down, in words, the time the scones were placed in the oven.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Ten minutes past two (1A time)
Mark 2: in the afternoon (1A afternoon)

Full-mark accepted descriptions:
- Ten minutes past two in the afternoon
- Ten past two in the afternoon
- Ten past two post meridiem (p.m.)
- Ten past two pm

questions.title: Mini-marathon and Irene town layout plan

subQuestions.questionText: Busisiwe participated in a Vhi Women's Mini Marathon. Using ANNEXURE A, write down the starting time of the mini-marathon using the 24-hour format.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1–2: $14{:}00$ (2A correct 24-hour time format)

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to ANNEXURE A in the question paper.) Determine the number of places where an ambulance can be found.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1–2: 8 (2A correct number)
subQuestions.topic: Maps and route plans – Reading from a map

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to ANNEXURE A.) State which mode of transport is NOT allowed on the mini-marathon route.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1–2: Bicycle (2RT bicycle)

subQuestions.label: 2.1.4(a)
subQuestions.questionText: The distance of a standard marathon is 42,2 km. Determine, in simplified form, what fraction of a standard marathon the Vhi Women's Mini Marathon is. (Mini-marathon distance = 9K + 1K = 10 km.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1 (in km):
Mark 1–2: Distance $= 9\text{K} + 1\text{K} = 10$ km (2A 10 km)
Mark 3: Fraction $= \frac{10}{42{,}2}$ (1MCA correct order)
Mark 4: $= \frac{50}{211}$ (1CA simplification)

OR Method 2 (in m):
Mark 1–2: Distance $= 1\,000 \times 10 = 10\,000$ m, $42{,}2$ km $= 42\,200$ m (2A 10 km)
Mark 3: Fraction $= \frac{10\,000}{42\,200}$ (1MCA correct order)
Mark 4: $= \frac{50}{211}$ (1CA simplification)

subQuestions.label: 2.1.4(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE reason why the Vhi Women's Mini Marathon is called a mini-marathon.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: Any acceptable explanation (2A explanation), e.g.:
- The distance is less than a full marathon.
- It is shorter than a standard marathon.
- It is a fraction of a full marathon.

subQuestions.questionText: Choose the answer and write only the letter (A–C) next to the question number. The probability of a runner crossing the railway line during the mini-marathon is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — 0% (2 marks)
The mini-marathon route does not cross the railway line, so the probability is 0%.

subQuestions.questionText: Busisiwe lives in Irene. ANNEXURE B shows the layout plan of Irene. Write down the place of interest that is situated at the corner of Krige Street and Bruce Street.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1–2: Scout House (2RT correct place of interest)

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to ANNEXURE B.) Give the general direction from Bastion Guest House to the Station & Shopping Centre.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: South-east OR SE (2A correct direction).
Accept: East of South.

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to ANNEXURE B.) Name the street that the railway lines cross.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: Nellmapius (2RT correct street).
Also accept: King OR Pioneer.

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to ANNEXURE B.) Give the name of the church found in King Street.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1–2: St Martin's Church (2RT correct church)

subQuestions.questionText: Busisiwe gives David the following travelling instructions to meet her: Drive from Irene Pre-Primary east along Crawford Street; Turn left into Queen Street; Take the first right into Stanley Street and continue to King Street; Turn right into King Street, pass five streets and then turn left; Continue across the first street. Before the next intersection Busisiwe will be waiting for David. Identify the place where Busisiwe will be waiting for David.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–3: Irene Library & Hall (3RT correct place).
[Accept Hall.]
subQuestions.topic: Following directions on a layout plan

subQuestions.questionText: The actual straight-line distance (as the crow flies) from the entrance of Irene Pre-Primary to the entrance of Irene Primary School is 1,9 km. Determine, rounded to the nearest thousand, the scale of the layout plan in the form $1 : \ldots$
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1 (km → cm):
Mark 1: Measured distance $= 8$ cm (1MA correct measurement)
Mark 2: $8$ cm : $1{,}9$ km (1MCA correct ratio)
Mark 3: $8$ cm : $190\,000$ cm (1C converting km to cm)
Mark 4: Scale $= 1 : 23\,750$ (1S simplified ratio)
Mark 5: $\approx 1 : 24\,000$ (1R correct rounding)

Accepted maximum-distance solution (8,4 cm):
$8{,}4$ cm : $1{,}9$ km → $8{,}4$ cm : $190\,000$ cm → $1 : 22\,619{,}05 \approx 1 : 23\,000$.

OR Method (cm → km):
Mark 1: 8,4 cm (1MA correct measurement)
Mark 2: $8{,}4$ cm $\div 100\,000 = 0{,}000084$ km (1C converting cm to km)
Mark 3: $0{,}000084$ km : $1{,}9$ km (1MCA correct ratio)
Mark 4: $1 : 22\,619$ (1S simplified ratio)
Mark 5: $\approx 1 : 23\,000$ (1R correct rounding)

[Provinces mark within ±1 mm of their provincial paper.]

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why a driver travelling along King Street cannot turn right into Bruce Street.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: Any reasonable opinion (2O opinion), e.g.:
- The traffic flow is in the opposite direction.
- One-way traffic / The arrow shows you can only turn left.
- The driver will be facing oncoming traffic.

subQuestions.questionText: Tshego is renovating her home. The rectangular window frame has outer dimensions: Length $A = 55$ cm, $B = 99$ cm and $C = 55$ cm; Width $= 149$ cm. Determine the perimeter of the rectangular window frame. (You may use: Perimeter of a rectangle $= 2(\text{length} + \text{width})$.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1:
Mark 1: Total length $= 55 + 99 + 55 = 209$ cm (1A total length)
Mark 2: Perimeter $= 2(209 + 149)$ cm (1SF substitution)
Mark 3: $= 2(358) = 716$ cm (1CA perimeter)

OR Method 2:
Mark 1: Total length identified (1A)
Mark 2: Perimeter $= (149 + 55 + 99 + 55 + 149 + 55 + 99 + 55)$ cm (1SF)
Mark 3: $= 716$ cm (1CA)

OR Method 3:
Mark 1: Total length identified (1A)
Mark 2: Perimeter $= 2(149) + 2(55+99+55)$ cm (1SF)
Mark 3: $= 298 + 418 = 716$ cm (1CA)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the inner area in $\text{cm}^2$ of the circular window frame. The inner diameter $= 605$ mm. (Use Area of a circle $= 3{,}142 \times (\text{radius})^2$.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1 (convert radius first):
Mark 1: Radius $= \frac{605}{2} = 302{,}5$ mm (1A radius)
Mark 2: $= 30{,}25$ cm (1C conversion)
Mark 3: Area $= 3{,}142 \times (30{,}25)^2$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 4: $= 2\,875{,}126375\ \text{cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)

OR Method 2 (calculate then convert):
Mark 1: Radius $= 302{,}5$ mm (1A)
Mark 2: Area $= 3{,}142 \times (302{,}5)^2 = 28\,512{,}6375\ \text{mm}^2$ (1SF)
Mark 3: $= 28\,751\,263{,}75 \div 100^2$ (1C conversion)
Mark 4: $= 2\,875{,}126375\ \text{cm}^2$ (1CA)
NPR (no penalty for correct rounding).

subQuestions.questionText: One of the windowpanes of the rectangular window frame broke. Write the probability, as a decimal, that it is NOT one of the windowpanes that can open. (4 of 7 windowpanes can open.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1:
Mark 1: Numerator $= 3$ (1A numerator — windowpanes that cannot open)
Mark 2: Denominator $= 7$ (1A denominator — total windowpanes)
Mark 3: $P = \frac{3}{7} = 0{,}4285714286$ (1CA decimal form)

OR Method 2:
Mark 1: $P = 1 - \frac{4}{7}$ (1M subtracting from 1)
Mark 2: $= \frac{3}{7}$ (1A simplification)
Mark 3: $= 0{,}4285714286$ (1CA decimal form)
NPR.

subQuestions.questionText: Tshego intends tiling the dining room and lounge floors. The dimensions of the lounge floor are 4 m by 5 m and of the dining room floor 3 m by 4 m. Show that the total floor area to be tiled is $32\ \text{m}^2$. (Use Area of a rectangle $= \text{length} \times \text{width}$.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Total area $= 4 \times 5 + 3 \times 4$ (1SF substitution of correct values)
Mark 2: $= 20 + 12 = 32\ \text{m}^2$ (1M adding)
NPU (no penalty for units).
[Candidates need not show $(20 + 12)\ \text{m}^2$ explicitly.]

subQuestions.questionText: Determine how many boxes of tiles Tshego will need if an extra 10% of the number of tiles must be added for cutting and breakages. Tile size: 35 cm by 35 cm. One box contains 4 tiles. Total floor area $= 32\ \text{m}^2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark allocation: 3 marks area of tile; 2 marks number of tiles; 2 marks adding 10% (tiles or area); 2 marks number of boxes.

Method 1:
Mark 1: Area of 1 tile $= 35 \times 35 = 1\,225\ \text{cm}^2$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2: $= 1\,225 \div 100^2\ \text{m}^2$ (1C conversion)
Mark 3: $= 0{,}1225\ \text{m}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: Number of tiles needed $= \frac{32}{0{,}1225}$ (1MCA dividing areas)
Mark 5: $= 261{,}2244898$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 6: Number to add $= 10\% \times 261{,}2244898 = 26{,}12244898$ (1MCA calculation 10%)
Mark 7: Total tiles $= 261{,}2244898 + 26{,}12244898 = 287{,}3469388$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 8: Number of boxes $= \frac{287{,}3469388}{4} = 71{,}83673469$ (1MCA dividing by 4)
Mark 9: $\therefore 72$ boxes (1CA rounding up)

OR alternative (rounding consistently up): $\Rightarrow 73$ boxes also accepted with corresponding mark allocation.

OR Method 3 (area covered per box):
Area of 1 tile $= (0{,}35)^2 = 0{,}1225\ \text{m}^2$; Area covered per box $= 0{,}1225 \times 4 = 0{,}49\ \text{m}^2$; Area to be tiled $= 32 \times 110\% = 35{,}2\ \text{m}^2$; Number of boxes $= \frac{35{,}2}{0{,}49} \approx 71{,}8 \Rightarrow 72$ boxes.

OR Method (per-room): Lounge tiles $= 12 \times 15 = 180$; Dining tiles $= 12 \times 9 = 108$; total $= 288$; with 10% $= 316{,}8 \approx 317$; boxes $= 317 \div 4 = 79{,}25 \approx 80$ boxes (also accepted for full marks per attached notes).

subQuestions.questionText: Show by means of calculations if Tshego's budget is enough to finish the tiling project. Costs: Tiles R143,84 per box of 4; Tile cement R99,90 per 20 kg bag (covers $3\ \text{m}^2$); 4 bags grout at R89,90 each; Labour R2 500; Budget R15 000.
subQuestions.memoText:
(CA from Q3.2.2 — using 72 boxes.)

Mark 1: Bags of tile cement $= \frac{32}{3} = 10{,}7 \approx 11$ (1A number of bags)
Mark 2: Cement cost $= 99{,}90 \times 11$ (1MCA multiplying cost with number)
Mark 3: $= \text{R}1\,098{,}90$ (1CA cement cost)
Mark 4: Grout cost $= 89{,}90 \times 4 = \text{R}359{,}60$ (1CA grout cost)
Mark 5: Tile cost $= 143{,}84 \times 72 = \text{R}10\,356{,}48$ (1CA tile cost)
Mark 6: Total $= 10\,356{,}48 + 1\,098{,}90 + 359{,}60 + 2\,500$ (1MCA adding 4 values)
Mark 7: $= \text{R}14\,314{,}98$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 8: Her budget is enough (R15 000 > R14 314,98; R685,02 to spare) (1O verification)

OR using 73 boxes: Tile cost $= 143{,}84 \times 73 = \text{R}10\,500{,}32$; Total $= \text{R}14\,458{,}82$; budget is still enough.

Mark allocation: 3 marks cement cost; 1 mark tile cost; 1 mark grout cost; 2 marks adding costs; 1 mark verification.

questions.title: Cinema seating and cylindrical diesel tank

subQuestions.questionText: ANNEXURE C shows the seating plan for a cinema during the Covid-19 pandemic. On which side of the cinema is seat E4 from seat E15 when a person is facing the screen?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: Right (2RT correct direction).
Also accept: East / E.

subQuestions.label: 4.1.2(a)
subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to ANNEXURE C.) Assume that pre-Covid-19 conditions apply and all the seats are occupied. Name the row and seat number of the middle seat in the 8th row from the screen.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Row K (1RT correct row)
Mark 2: Seat 11 (1RT correct seat)
Final answer: K11.

subQuestions.label: 4.1.2(b)
subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to ANNEXURE C.) Write down the ratio of the number of wheelchair spaces to the number of seats for patrons NOT in wheelchairs.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Total seats $= 10 + 16 \times 5 + 19 + 21 = 130$ (1A total seats)
Mark 2: Ratio $= 4 : 130$ (1MCA ratio in correct order)
Mark 3: $= 2 : 65$ (1CA simplification)

OR: Total seats $= 64 + 66\ (\text{vacant}) = 130$; same ratio of $4 : 130 = 2 : 65$.

Accept $4 : 130$ or $2 : 65$ for full marks. Accept simplified unit ratios. If $4 : (\text{incorrect 2nd part})$ without working shown, max 2 marks if simplified correctly.

subQuestions.questionText: On Friday evenings, pre-Covid-19, all the seats in the cinema (excluding the wheelchair spaces) were always occupied. Calculate the percentage income lost due to social distancing during the pandemic if ALL the tickets for the seats are equally priced.
subQuestions.memoText:
(CA from Q4.1.2 total seats = 130.)

Method 1:
Mark 1: Total vacant seats $= 66$ (1A total vacant seats)
Mark 2: $\% \text{ income lost} = \frac{66}{130} \times 100\%$ (1MCA percentage calculation)
Mark 3: $= 50{,}76923077 \approx 50{,}77\%$ (1CA simplification)

OR Method 2:
Mark 1: $\% \text{ from occupied} = \frac{64}{130} \times 100\% \approx 49{,}23\%$ (1CA)
Mark 2: $\% \text{ lost} = 100\% - 49{,}23\%$ (1MCA subtracting from 100%)
Mark 3: $= 50{,}77\%$ (1CA)
NPR.

subQuestions.questionText: The cinema owners use a generator powered by diesel stored in a cylindrical tank. State the purpose of the breathing valve on the tank.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: Any reasonable answer (2O reason), e.g.:
- To allow air inside the tank to escape as the diesel is pumped in.
- To release air bubbles formed.
- To let air in.
- To protect the tank from exploding or imploding.

subQuestions.label: 4.2.2(a)
subQuestions.questionText: The steel used to make the tank is 5 mm thick all around. The outer diameter is 3,22 m. Show that the inner diameter of the tank is 3,21 m.
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1:
Mark 1: Inner diameter $= 3{,}22 - 2 \times \frac{5}{1\,000}$ m (1A subtracting double the thickness)
Mark 2: $= 3{,}21$ m (1C converting to m)

OR Method 2:
Mark 1: $5 + 5 = \frac{10}{1\,000} = 0{,}01$ m (1A subtracting double the thickness)
Mark 2: Inner diameter $= 3{,}22 - 0{,}01 = 3{,}21$ m (1C converting to m)

subQuestions.label: 4.2.2(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the maximum litres of diesel that this tank can hold according to safety regulations. The tank is filled to 95% of its capacity. The steel is 5 mm thick. Outer height (length) = 7,25 m. Use Volume of a cylinder $= 3{,}142 \times (\text{radius})^2 \times \text{height}$, and $1\ \text{m}^3 = 1\,000\ \ell$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Inner height $= 7{,}25 - 2 \times \frac{5}{1\,000}$ m (1MA subtracting double the thickness)
Mark 2: $= 7{,}24$ m (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: Radius $= \frac{3{,}21}{2} = 1{,}605$ m (1MCA finding radius)
Mark 4: Volume $= 3{,}142 \times (1{,}605)^2 \times 7{,}24$ (1SF correct values)
Mark 5: $= 58{,}599622782\ \text{m}^3$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 6: Filling volume $= 58{,}599622782 \times 95\%$ (1MCA percentage finding)
Mark 7: $= 55{,}6696416429\ \text{m}^3$ (1CA capacity)
Mark 8: $\times 1\,000 = 55\,669{,}64\ \ell$ (1C to litres)

subQuestions.questionText: The external surface area of the tank, excluding the base area of the external attachments ($1\ \text{m}^2$), needs to be painted. The spread rate is $3\ \text{m}^2/\ell$. The manager states he would need less than 30 litres of paint. Verify, by showing ALL calculations, whether the manager is CORRECT. Use SA $= 2 \times 3{,}142 \times r(r + h)$.
subQuestions.memoText:
(CA from Q4.2.2.)

Method 1:
Mark 1: Radius $\approx 1{,}61$ m (1MCA correct radius)
Mark 2: SA $= 2 \times 3{,}142 \times 1{,}61 \times (1{,}61 + 7{,}25)$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 3: $\approx 89{,}64\ \text{m}^2$ (1S simplification)
Mark 4: Total area to be painted $= 89{,}64 - 1$ (1MCA subtracting $1\ \text{m}^2$)
Mark 5: $= 88{,}64\ \text{m}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 6: Litres needed $= 88{,}64 \div 3$ (1MCA dividing by 3)
Mark 7: $= 29{,}55$ litres (1CA simplification)
Mark 8: Manager is CORRECT (29,55 ℓ < 30 ℓ) (1O verification — Valid)

OR Method 2:
SA $\approx 89{,}64\ \text{m}^2$; subtract $1\ \text{m}^2$ → $88{,}64\ \text{m}^2$; area covered by 30 ℓ $= 30 \times 3 = 90\ \text{m}^2$; less is needed → manager CORRECT.

questions.title: Bakkie, garage and Springbok–Windhoek strip chart

subQuestions.questionText: Letitia buys a new bakkie. Bakkie dimensions: Width = 1 860 mm, Length = 5 362 mm, Height = 1 815 mm. Identify which view of the bakkie is represented by the dimensions 1 815 mm × 1 860 mm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: Front view OR Back view OR Rear view (2RT view).
The height (1 815 mm) and width (1 860 mm) are the dimensions visible when looking at the bakkie from the front or back.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the value of D (the space between the sides of the bakkie and the side walls of the garage) if the bakkie is parked exactly in the middle of the garage. Garage inner width = 3,6 m. Bakkie width = 1 860 mm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1 (in metres):
Mark 1: Width of the bakkie $= 1{,}86$ m (1C conversion)
Mark 2: $2D = 3{,}6 - 1{,}86 = 1{,}74$ m (1MA difference)
Mark 3: $D = \frac{1{,}74}{2}$ (1MCA dividing by 2)
Mark 4: $= 0{,}87$ m (1CA simplification)

OR Method 2 (in mm):
Mark 1: Width of garage $= 3\,600$ mm (1C conversion)
Mark 2: $2D = 3\,600 - 1\,860 = 1\,740$ mm (1MA difference)
Mark 3: $D = \frac{1\,740}{2}$ (1MCA dividing by 2)
Mark 4: $= 870$ mm (1CA simplification)

subQuestions.questionText: Letitia needs to choose a colour and window tint. The bakkie comes in four colours: white, black, blue and green. The windows can be tinted using 35% tint or 50% tint. State how many different choices there are for this bakkie.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $4 \times 2$ (1MA multiplying)
Mark 2: $= 8$ choices (1CA number of choices)

subQuestions.questionText: Letitia studied a strip chart connecting Springbok in South Africa with Windhoek in Namibia (ANNEXURE D shows the strip chart). State ONE difference between a strip chart and a normal road map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1–2: Any acceptable statement (2A statement), e.g.:
- A map is drawn to scale while a strip chart is not.
- A map shows the routes in a winding manner while a strip chart shows them as straight lines.
subQuestions.topic: Maps – Strip charts vs road maps

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to ANNEXURE D.) Determine the distance between Springbok and Gobabis.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: 892 km identified (1RT correct 892)
Mark 2: $892 + 203$ (1RT adding)
Mark 3: $= 1\,095$ km (1CA distance in km)
[CA considered only if adding distance from strip chart other than 203 km, then max 2 marks.]
subQuestions.topic: Maps – Reading distances from a strip chart

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the Namibian town found on the border between South Africa and Namibia.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1–2: Noordoewer (2RT correct town)

subQuestions.label: 5.2.4(a)
subQuestions.questionText: Letitia undertook the following trip: She left Solitaire at 04:00 and travelled 140 km south on C14. She then turned right and travelled 289 km east on C19. At Mariental she turned, then drove to Keetmanshoop and arrived at 12:25. Calculate the total distance Letitia travelled during this trip.
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1:
Mark 1: Distance Mariental to Keetmanshoop $= 644 - 427 = 217$ km (1RT distances)
Mark 2: $140 + 289 + 217$ (1A simplification)
Mark 3: $= 646$ km (1CA distance)

OR Method 2:
Mark 1: $140 + 289 + (465 - 248)$ (1RT distances)
Mark 2: $= 140 + 289 + 217$ (1A simplification)
Mark 3: $= 646$ km (1CA distance)

subQuestions.label: 5.2.4(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Letitia travelled on different types of roads and she maintained the average speed limit prescribed for these types of roads. She stopped three times during the trip to take a break. Letitia stated that the three breaks were approximately 25 minutes each. Verify, with calculations, whether Letitia's statement is CORRECT. Use $\text{Time} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Speed}}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
